items.mnemonic_text: The space (間) gone wrong (違): a mistake.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>space between</kanji> two pigeonhole dividers is a mail slot, and you shove your letter into the one that <kanji>differs</kanji> from yours by a single room number. Feeding that wrong slot is what it means to <vocabulary>make a mistake</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 電車を間違えて、知らない町に行ってしまいました。
example_sentences.english: I got on the wrong train and ended up in a town I didn't know.
example_sentences.furigana: 電[でん]車[しゃ]を間[ま]違[ちが]えて、知[し]らない町[まち]に行[い]ってしまいました。

example_sentences.japanese: 喫茶店の店員は、いつも私の名前を間違えます。
example_sentences.english: The clerk at the coffee shop always gets my name wrong.
example_sentences.furigana: 喫[きっ]茶[さ]店[てん]の店[てん]員[いん]は、いつも私[わたし]の名[な]前[まえ]を間[ま]違[ちが]えます。

example_sentences.japanese: 塩と砂糖を間違えないでください。
example_sentences.english: Please don't mix up the salt and the sugar.
example_sentences.furigana: 塩[しお]と砂[さ]糖[とう]を間[ま]違[ちが]えないでください。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 間（ま）＋違（ちが）＋う.
items.mnemonic_text: Falling into the wrong gap: machigau.
items.meaning_mnemonic: When the <kanji form="間">gap between</kanji> what you believe and what is true turns out to <kanji form="違">differ</kanji>, you are <vocabulary form="間違う">mistaken</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: この地図は間違っていますよ。
example_sentences.english: This map is wrong, you know.
example_sentences.furigana: この地[ち]図[ず]は間違[まちが]っていますよ。

example_sentences.japanese: 数学のテストで、答えが一つだけ間違っていました。
example_sentences.english: On the math test, only one answer was wrong.
example_sentences.furigana: 数[すう]学[がく]のテストで、答[こた]えが一[ひと]つだけ間違[まちが]っていました。

example_sentences.japanese: 間違ってもいいですから、日本語で話してください。
example_sentences.english: It's fine to get it wrong, so please speak in Japanese.
example_sentences.furigana: 間違[まちが]ってもいいですから、日本[にほん]語[ご]で話[はな]してください。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 修（しゅう）＋理（り）＋する, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Cultivating (修) the logic (理) back: to repair.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="修">discipline</kanji> a broken machine part by part until every piece lines up with its own <kanji form="理">logic</kanji> again, and that is to <vocabulary form="修理する">repair</vocabulary> it.

example_sentences.japanese: 兄は壊れたラジオを修理するのが得意です。
example_sentences.english: My older brother is good at repairing broken radios.
example_sentences.furigana: 兄[あに]は壊[こわ]れたラジオを修[しゅう]理[り]するのが得[とく]意[い]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 冷蔵庫が動かないので、明日修理する人が来ます。
example_sentences.english: The fridge isn't working, so someone is coming tomorrow to repair it.
example_sentences.furigana: 冷[れい]蔵[ぞう]庫[こ]が動[うご]かないので、明日[あした]修[しゅう]理[り]する人[ひと]が来[き]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 古い靴を修理する店が、駅の近くにあります。
example_sentences.english: There's a shop near the station that repairs old shoes.
example_sentences.furigana: 古[ふる]い靴[くつ]を修[しゅう]理[り]する店[みせ]が、駅[えき]の近[ちか]くにあります。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 掛（か）＋かる.
items.mnemonic_text: Hanging in the balance: kakaru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A coat on a hook stays put with no one holding it, and an hour spent on a job slips by the same way. Either one just <vocabulary form="掛かる">hangs</vocabulary> there and takes the time it takes.
items.reading_mnemonic: A crow perches on the coat that <vocabulary form="掛かる">hangs</vocabulary> on its hook with no one holding it, and croaks <reading>caw-caw-roo</reading>, <reading>かかる</reading>, once for every hour the job takes.

example_sentences.japanese: 家から駅まで歩いて二十分掛かります。
example_sentences.english: It takes twenty minutes to walk from home to the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 家[いえ]から駅[えき]まで歩[ある]いて二[に]十[じゅう]分[ふん]掛[か]かります。

example_sentences.japanese: 引っ越すのに、お金がたくさん掛かりました。
example_sentences.english: Moving cost a lot of money.
example_sentences.furigana: 引[ひ]っ越[こ]すのに、お金[かね]がたくさん掛[か]かりました。

example_sentences.japanese: 部屋には母の絵が掛かっています。
example_sentences.english: My mother's painting hangs in the room.
example_sentences.furigana: 部屋[へや]には母[はは]の絵[え]が掛[か]かっています。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 掛（か）＋ける.
items.mnemonic_text: Hanging something up: kakeru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You reach up and set the frame on the nail yourself; you choose to put a full hour into the work. Doing either by your own hand is to <vocabulary form="掛ける">hang</vocabulary> a thing or spend the time on it.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already met 掛かる, so its hands-on twin <vocabulary form="掛ける">to hang or spend</vocabulary> is simply <reading>かける</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 帰ったら、コートはここに掛けてください。
example_sentences.english: When you get home, hang your coat here.
example_sentences.furigana: 帰[かえ]ったら、コートはここに掛[か]けてください。

example_sentences.japanese: 弟はいつも椅子に服を掛けておきます。
example_sentences.english: My younger brother always leaves his clothes hanging over the chair.
example_sentences.furigana: 弟[おとうと]はいつも椅[い]子[す]に服[ふく]を掛[か]けておきます。

example_sentences.japanese: この料理には時間を掛けました。
example_sentences.english: I put a lot of time into this dish.
example_sentences.furigana: この料[りょう]理[り]には時[じ]間[かん]を掛[か]けました。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 重（かさ）＋なる.
items.mnemonic_text: Heavy loads stacking themselves: kasanaru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Loose sheets keep drifting down onto each other with no hand guiding them, and the stack grows <kanji form="重">heavy</kanji> as each one lands. Left to themselves they <vocabulary form="重なる">overlap</vocabulary> and settle into a pile.
items.reading_mnemonic: A dancer clacks her <reading>castanets</reading> over the desk, and with every clack another loose sheet drifts down onto the last until they <vocabulary form="重なる">overlap</vocabulary> in a heavy pile: <reading>かさなる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 会議と約束の時間が重なってしまいました。
example_sentences.english: The meeting ended up at the same time as my appointment.
example_sentences.furigana: 会[かい]議[ぎ]と約[やく]束[そく]の時[じ]間[かん]が重[かさ]なってしまいました。

example_sentences.japanese: 机の上に本が重なっています。
example_sentences.english: Books are piled up on the desk.
example_sentences.furigana: 机[つくえ]の上[うえ]に本[ほん]が重[かさ]なっています。

example_sentences.japanese: 仕事が重なって、今週はとても忙しいです。
example_sentences.english: Work has piled up, so I'm very busy this week.
example_sentences.furigana: 仕[し]事[ごと]が重[かさ]なって、今[こん]週[しゅう]はとても忙[いそが]しいです。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 重（かさ）＋ねる.
items.mnemonic_text: Stacking heavy loads on purpose: kasaneru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You set plate on plate by hand, squaring each one on the last, every <kanji form="重">heavy</kanji> disc pushing the stack down harder. Doing it on purpose like that is to <vocabulary form="重ねる">pile up</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already met 重なる, so its by-hand partner <vocabulary form="重ねる">to pile things up</vocabulary> is simply <reading>かさねる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 食べた後で、皿を重ねて台所に運んでください。
example_sentences.english: After eating, please stack the plates and carry them to the kitchen.
example_sentences.furigana: 食[た]べた後[あと]で、皿[さら]を重[かさ]ねて台[だい]所[どころ]に運[はこ]んでください。

example_sentences.japanese: 寒い日は、シャツを二枚重ねて着ます。
example_sentences.english: On cold days, I wear two shirts, one over the other.
example_sentences.furigana: 寒[さむ]い日[ひ]は、シャツを二[に]枚[まい]重[かさ]ねて着[き]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 箱を三つ重ねたら、猫がその上に座った。
example_sentences.english: When I stacked three boxes, the cat sat on top of them.
example_sentences.furigana: 箱[はこ]を三[みっ]つ重[かさ]ねたら、猫[ねこ]がその上[うえ]に座[すわ]った。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 知（し）＋らせる.
items.mnemonic_text: Making someone know: shiraseru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>know</kanji> a fact the moment your arrow thuds into the target. Firing that same fact into someone else's target is <vocabulary>to inform / notify</vocabulary> them.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already learned 知 is 「し」 back in 知る, so <vocabulary>to inform / notify</vocabulary> someone is just <reading>しらせる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 会議の場所が変わったことを、みんなに知らせるのを忘れた。
example_sentences.english: I forgot to tell everyone that the meeting place had changed.
example_sentences.furigana: 会[かい]議[ぎ]の場[ば]所[しょ]が変[か]わったことを、みんなに知[し]らせるのを忘[わす]れた。

example_sentences.japanese: 赤ちゃんが生まれたら、姉は電話で知らせると言っていた。
example_sentences.english: My older sister said she'd call to let us know when the baby is born.
example_sentences.furigana: 赤[あか]ちゃんが生[う]まれたら、姉[あね]は電[でん]話[わ]で知[し]らせると言[い]っていた。

example_sentences.japanese: 授業に遅れるときは、先生に知らせるほうがいいですよ。
example_sentences.english: If you're going to be late for class, you should let your teacher know.
example_sentences.furigana: 授[じゅ]業[ぎょう]に遅[おく]れるときは、先[せん]生[せい]に知[し]らせるほうがいいですよ。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 届（とど）＋け＋出（で）＋る.
items.mnemonic_text: Delivering a notice out: todokederu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="届">deliver</kanji> a completed form to the city office and let it <kanji form="出">leave</kanji> your hands for good; that is to <vocabulary form="届け出る">report</vocabulary> or file something officially.

example_sentences.japanese: 財布を無くしたので、交番に届け出ました。
example_sentences.english: I lost my wallet, so I reported it at the police box.
example_sentences.furigana: 財[さい]布[ふ]を無[な]くしたので、交[こう]番[ばん]に届[とど]け出[で]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 引っ越したら、新しい住所を市に届け出なければなりません。
example_sentences.english: When you move, you have to report your new address to the city.
example_sentences.furigana: 引[ひ]っ越[こ]したら、新[あたら]しい住[じゅう]所[しょ]を市[し]に届[とど]け出[で]なければなりません。

example_sentences.japanese: 会社を休むときは、前の日に届け出てください。
example_sentences.english: If you're taking a day off work, please file notice the day before.
example_sentences.furigana: 会[かい]社[しゃ]を休[やす]むときは、前[まえ]の日[ひ]に届[とど]け出[で]てください。

items.reading_composition: On'yomi — 信（しん）＋じる.
items.mnemonic_text: A person's word (言) trusted: shinjiru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: To take another person's word as plain <kanji form="信">truth</kanji>, with no proof in your hand, is to <vocabulary form="信じる">believe</vocabulary> them.

example_sentences.japanese: 私の言葉を信じる人は、弟だけでした。
example_sentences.english: The only one who believed what I said was my little brother.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の言[こと]葉[ば]を信[しん]じる人[ひと]は、弟[おとうと]だけでした。

example_sentences.japanese: 母はいつも「自分の力を信じる」と言っています。
example_sentences.english: My mom always says, "Believe in your own strength."
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]はいつも「自[じ]分[ぶん]の力[ちから]を信[しん]じる」と言[い]っています。

example_sentences.japanese: 猫が冷蔵庫を開けた話は、誰も信じるはずがない。
example_sentences.english: There's no way anyone will believe the story about the cat opening the fridge.
example_sentences.furigana: 猫[ねこ]が冷[れい]蔵[ぞう]庫[こ]を開[あ]けた話[はなし]は、誰[だれ]も信[しん]じるはずがない。

items.word_type: ichidan verb, transitive verb, intransitive verb
items.reading_composition: On'yomi — 感（かん）＋じる.
items.mnemonic_text: The heart's field stirred: kanjiru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="感">emotion</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="感じる">to feel</vocabulary> word are the same; the added kana just turns that emotion into something you actively do.

example_sentences.japanese: 冬の朝、窓を開けたときに感じる冷たい風が好きです。
example_sentences.english: I love the cold air you feel when you open the window on a winter morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 冬[ふゆ]の朝[あさ]、窓[まど]を開[あ]けたときに感[かん]じる冷[つめ]たい風[かぜ]が好[す]きです。

example_sentences.japanese: 新しい町に引っ越してから、少し寂しく感じる日が多い。
example_sentences.english: Since moving to a new town, I often have days when I feel a little lonely.
example_sentences.furigana: 新[あたら]しい町[まち]に引[ひ]っ越[こ]してから、少[すこ]し寂[さび]しく感[かん]じる日[ひ]が多[おお]い。

example_sentences.japanese: 試験の前は、一時間がとても短く感じる。
example_sentences.english: Right before an exam, an hour feels really short.
example_sentences.furigana: 試[し]験[けん]の前[まえ]は、一[いち]時[じ]間[かん]がとても短[みじか]く感[かん]じる。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 提（てい）＋出（しゅつ）＋する, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Presenting (提) and putting out (出): to submit.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The finished report stays in your hands until you <kanji form="提">carry</kanji> it to the front desk and let it <kanji form="出">leave</kanji> your fingers onto the tray. Letting a document exit you and stay with the office is how you <vocabulary form="提出する">submit</vocabulary> it.

example_sentences.japanese: 銀行の窓口で書類を提出しました。
example_sentences.english: I handed in the documents at the bank counter.
example_sentences.furigana: 銀[ぎん]行[こう]の窓[まど]口[ぐち]で書[しょ]類[るい]を提[てい]出[しゅつ]しました。

example_sentences.japanese: 名前を書いてから提出してください。
example_sentences.english: Please write your name before you hand it in.
example_sentences.furigana: 名[な]前[まえ]を書[か]いてから提[てい]出[しゅつ]してください。

example_sentences.japanese: テストを提出した後で、答えを一つ間違えたことが分かった。
example_sentences.english: After turning in the test, I realized I'd gotten one answer wrong.
example_sentences.furigana: テストを提[てい]出[しゅつ]した後[あと]で、答[こた]えを一[ひと]つ間[ま]違[ちが]えたことが分[わ]かった。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 申（もう）＋し＋込（こ）＋む.
items.mnemonic_text: Speaking your request into the pile: moushikomu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You fill in your name and push the sheet into the <kanji form="込">crowded</kanji> stack of everyone else's forms on the counter. Adding yourself to that packed pile is how you <vocabulary form="申し込む">apply</vocabulary> for a place.

example_sentences.japanese: 来月の日本語の試験に申し込みました。
example_sentences.english: I signed up for next month's Japanese exam.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]月[げつ]の日本[にほん]語[ご]の試[し]験[けん]に申[もう]し込[こ]みました。

example_sentences.japanese: 電話でも申し込むことができますよ。
example_sentences.english: You can apply by phone, too.
example_sentences.furigana: 電[でん]話[わ]でも申[もう]し込[こ]むことができますよ。

example_sentences.japanese: 早く申し込まなければ、席が無くなるかもしれません。
example_sentences.english: If you don't sign up soon, the seats might run out.
example_sentences.furigana: 早[はや]く申[もう]し込[こ]まなければ、席[せき]が無[な]くなるかもしれません。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 申（もう）＋す.
items.mnemonic_text: A humble mouth speaking upward: mousu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You bend low and aim your words at the floor near an important person's feet, so they reach that person from below. Speaking from down there, kept small on purpose, is to <vocabulary form="申す">say something humbly</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Bowed so low your words land by the chairman's feet, you speak up to him like a <reading>mouse</reading> squeaking from the floor: <reading>もうす</reading>, to <vocabulary form="申す">say</vocabulary> something humbly.

example_sentences.japanese: はじめまして、山田と申します。
example_sentences.english: Nice to meet you. My name is Yamada.
example_sentences.furigana: はじめまして、山田[やまだ]と申[もう]します。

example_sentences.japanese: 母が「ありがとう」と申していました。
example_sentences.english: My mother asked me to tell you thank you.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]が「ありがとう」と申[もう]していました。

example_sentences.japanese: 一つ意見を申してもいいですか。
example_sentences.english: May I offer one opinion?
example_sentences.furigana: 一[ひと]つ意[い]見[けん]を申[もう]してもいいですか。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 致（いた）＋す.
items.mnemonic_text: A humble hand reaching to serve: itasu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A servant finishes every task before anyone notices it needed doing, then sweeps away their own footprints so no one sees the work. Getting the whole job done while keeping yourself invisible is to <vocabulary form="致す">do it, humbly</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Two overalled helpers answer every call at the back door with a soft <reading>it's us</reading>, then quietly fix whatever broke and slip out again. Doing the work for someone while staying that far in the background is <vocabulary form="致す">to do, humbly</vocabulary>, spoken as <reading>いたす</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 夕方、もう一度電話致します。
example_sentences.english: I'll call you once more this evening.
example_sentences.furigana: 夕[ゆう]方[がた]、もう一[いち]度[ど]電[でん]話[わ]致[いた]します。

example_sentences.japanese: 料理は私が致しますので、テレビでも見ていてください。
example_sentences.english: I'll take care of the cooking, so why not watch some TV?
example_sentences.furigana: 料[りょう]理[り]は私[わたし]が致[いた]しますので、テレビでも見[み]ていてください。

example_sentences.japanese: 飲み物はコーヒーに致します。
example_sentences.english: For my drink, I'll have coffee.
example_sentences.furigana: 飲[の]み物[もの]はコーヒーに致[いた]します。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 参（まい）＋る.
items.mnemonic_text: Bowing low on the way: mairu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You leave the car at the gate and walk the last stretch up to the house on foot, hat held in both hands. Coming toward someone that plainly, on foot and uncovered, is to <vocabulary form="参る">come to them humbly</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: An old retainer waves away every offer of a ride, saying that walking to you in person is <reading>my rule</reading>, and sets off down the full length of the road. That slow arrival on your own two feet is <vocabulary form="参る">to go and come humbly</vocabulary>, said as <reading>まいる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 明日の朝十時に、駅まで参ります。
example_sentences.english: I'll come to the station at ten tomorrow morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]の朝[あさ]十[じゅう]時[じ]に、駅[えき]まで参[まい]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: 電車が参ります。危ないですから、下がってください。
example_sentences.english: A train is arriving. It's dangerous, so please step back.
example_sentences.furigana: 電[でん]車[しゃ]が参[まい]ります。危[あぶ]ないですから、下[さ]がってください。

example_sentences.japanese: 母はすぐ参りますので、こちらの椅子に座ってください。
example_sentences.english: My mother will be right here, so please have a seat in this chair.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]はすぐ参[まい]りますので、こちらの椅[い]子[す]に座[すわ]ってください。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 伺（うかが）＋う.
items.mnemonic_text: A person (亻) watching (司) respectfully: ukagau.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You knock softly and wait outside the doorway until someone waves you in, then lean your head through to put your question. Approaching a person's home and their attention that carefully is to <vocabulary form="伺う">visit and ask humbly</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A polite <reading>kangaroo</reading> props its paws on the garden fence and waits to be waved through before hopping in to ask after your health. Peeking in and raising a question that gently is <vocabulary form="伺う">to visit and ask humbly</vocabulary>, which comes out as <reading>うかがう</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 来週の火曜日に、そちらへ伺ってもいいですか。
example_sentences.english: May I come and visit you next Tuesday?
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]週[しゅう]の火[か]曜[よう]日[び]に、そちらへ伺[うかが]ってもいいですか。

example_sentences.japanese: そのお話は、会議の後でゆっくり伺います。
example_sentences.english: I'll hear about that properly after the meeting.
example_sentences.furigana: そのお話[はなし]は、会[かい]議[ぎ]の後[あと]でゆっくり伺[うかが]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 駅員に道を伺ったら、親切に教えてくれました。
example_sentences.english: When I asked the station staff for directions, they explained kindly.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]員[いん]に道[みち]を伺[うかが]ったら、親[しん]切[せつ]に教[おし]えてくれました。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 拝（はい）＋見（けん）＋する, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Bowing (拝) to view (見): to humbly look.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You bow so low over the offered document that your <kanji form="見">seeing</kanji> eye has to peer up at it from just above the floor. Looking at what someone shows you from that far down is how you <vocabulary form="拝見する">see it, humbly</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、お手紙を拝見しました。
example_sentences.english: I read your letter yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]、お手[て]紙[がみ]を拝[はい]見[けん]しました。

example_sentences.japanese: すみません、切符を拝見します。
example_sentences.english: Excuse me, may I see your ticket?
example_sentences.furigana: すみません、切[きっ]符[ぷ]を拝[はい]見[けん]します。

example_sentences.japanese: おじいさんの古い写真を拝見して、とても驚きました。
example_sentences.english: I was really surprised when I saw your grandfather's old photos.
example_sentences.furigana: おじいさんの古[ふる]い写[しゃ]真[しん]を拝[はい]見[けん]して、とても驚[おどろ]きました。

items.reading_composition: On'yomi — ご＋覧（らん）＋になる.
items.mnemonic_text: Honorific viewing: goran ni naru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You set the photo album on a stand and step back with folded hands, offering it up the way a gallery presents its finest piece. Letting an honored person <vocabulary form="ご覧になる">see something, honorifically</vocabulary>, means presenting it to them like that.

example_sentences.japanese: 先生がご覧になる前に、この絵を直しておきましょう。
example_sentences.english: Let's fix this drawing before the teacher sees it.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]がご覧[らん]になる前[まえ]に、この絵[え]を直[なお]しておきましょう。

example_sentences.japanese: 右の窓からご覧になる海は、とてもきれいですよ。
example_sentences.english: The sea you'll see from the window on your right is really beautiful.
example_sentences.furigana: 右[みぎ]の窓[まど]からご覧[らん]になる海[うみ]は、とてもきれいですよ。

example_sentences.japanese: おばあさんは毎朝、庭の花をご覧になるのが好きです。
example_sentences.english: The old lady loves looking at the flowers in the garden every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: おばあさんは毎[まい]朝[あさ]、庭[にわ]の花[はな]をご覧[らん]になるのが好[す]きです。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 召（め）＋し＋上（あ）＋がる.
items.mnemonic_text: Calling something up to eat: meshiagaru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: An honored guest never fetches their own meal: the dishes are <kanji form="召">called for</kanji> from the kitchen and carried <kanji form="上">up</kanji> to the head of the table. Eating and drinking what has been summoned and raised to you is to <vocabulary form="召し上がる">eat or drink, honorifically</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: お茶とコーヒー、どちらを召し上がりますか。
example_sentences.english: Which would you like, tea or coffee?
example_sentences.furigana: お茶[ちゃ]とコーヒー、どちらを召[め]し上[あ]がりますか。

example_sentences.japanese: 先生は昼ご飯に弁当を召し上がりました。
example_sentences.english: The teacher had a boxed lunch for lunch.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]は昼[ひる]ご飯[はん]に弁[べん]当[とう]を召[め]し上[あ]がりました。

example_sentences.japanese: 熱いので、ゆっくり召し上がってください。
example_sentences.english: It's hot, so please take your time with it.
example_sentences.furigana: 熱[あつ]いので、ゆっくり召[め]し上[あ]がってください。

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: The all-purpose respectful verb: irassharu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The white-gloved <reading>usher</reading> at the theatre glides over to walk each important guest in, out, and to their seat without a wasted step. That smooth, honored coming and going is <vocabulary form="いらっしゃる">to be, go, or come, honorifically</vocabulary>, and it sounds like <reading>いらっしゃる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 来週、先生のご主人が日本にいらっしゃいます。
example_sentences.english: My teacher's husband is coming to Japan next week.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]週[しゅう]、先[せん]生[せい]のご主[しゅ]人[じん]が日本[にほん]にいらっしゃいます。

example_sentences.japanese: おばあさんは今、庭にいらっしゃいますよ。
example_sentences.english: Grandma is out in the garden right now.
example_sentences.furigana: おばあさんは今[いま]、庭[にわ]にいらっしゃいますよ。

example_sentences.japanese: どちらからいらっしゃいましたか。
example_sentences.english: Where have you come from?
example_sentences.furigana: どちらからいらっしゃいましたか。

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: The respectful way to speak: ossharu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Whatever slow <reading>oh, sure</reading> the old retired professor mutters from his armchair, the whole class copies into their notes as settled fact. Giving a statement that weight because of who spoke it is <vocabulary form="おっしゃる">to say, honorifically</vocabulary>, and the sound is <reading>おっしゃる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: すみません、もっとゆっくりおっしゃってください。
example_sentences.english: Sorry, could you say that a bit more slowly?
example_sentences.furigana: すみません、もっとゆっくりおっしゃってください。

example_sentences.japanese: お名前は何とおっしゃいますか。
example_sentences.english: May I ask your name?
example_sentences.furigana: お名[な]前[まえ]は何[なに]とおっしゃいますか。

example_sentences.japanese: 奥さんは、この料理が一番おいしいとおっしゃいました。
example_sentences.english: His wife said this dish was the most delicious.
example_sentences.furigana: 奥[おく]さんは、この料[りょう]理[り]が一[いち]番[ばん]おいしいとおっしゃいました。

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: The respectful way to do: nasaru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: When the grand duchess Nessa decides a thing will happen, it happens — <reading>Nessa rules</reading> the whole estate, and whatever task she takes on, she personally <vocabulary form="なさる">does the action, honorifically</vocabulary>. The sound of that lands as <reading>なさる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 週末は何をなさいますか。
example_sentences.english: What are you doing this weekend?
example_sentences.furigana: 週[しゅう]末[まつ]は何[なに]をなさいますか。

example_sentences.japanese: お父さんは日曜日も仕事をなさるんですか。
example_sentences.english: Does your father work on Sundays too?
example_sentences.furigana: お父[とう]さんは日[にち]曜[よう]日[び]も仕[し]事[ごと]をなさるんですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 来月、ご家族と旅行をなさるそうですね。
example_sentences.english: I hear you're taking a trip with your family next month.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]月[げつ]、ご家[か]族[ぞく]と旅[りょ]行[こう]をなさるそうですね。

items.reading_composition: On'yomi — ご＋存（ぞん）＋じ.
items.mnemonic_text: Respectfully preserving knowledge: gozonji.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A fact your honored guest is already <kanji form="存">aware of</kanji> was sitting in their head before you spoke. Something that already <kanji form="存">exists</kanji> in a superior's mind before it is said is the honored form of <vocabulary form="ご存じ">knowing</vocabulary> it.

example_sentences.japanese: この近くに郵便局があるか、ご存じですか。
example_sentences.english: Do you know if there's a post office near here?
example_sentences.furigana: この近[ちか]くに郵[ゆう]便[びん]局[きょく]があるか、ご存[ぞん]じですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 駅員なら、バスの時間をご存じだと思います。
example_sentences.english: The station staff should know the bus times.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]員[いん]なら、バスの時[じ]間[かん]をご存[ぞん]じだと思[おも]います。

example_sentences.japanese: あの方は日本の歴史をよくご存じです。
example_sentences.english: That gentleman knows Japanese history very well.
example_sentences.furigana: あの方[ほう]は日本[にほん]の歴[れき]史[し]をよくご存[ぞん]じです。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 頂（いただ）＋く.
items.mnemonic_text: Receiving something atop your head: itadaku.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You take the gift in both hands and lift it up past your forehead, putting yourself lower than the thing you were just given. Receiving or eating anything from that bowed-under position is to <vocabulary form="頂く">receive it, humbly</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the shrine a tame duck waddles up and drops a rice cracker into your cupped hands, and you bow lower than the bird to take it. That <reading>eat a duck</reading> moment, receiving with your head down, is <vocabulary form="頂く">to receive and eat, humbly</vocabulary>, said as <reading>いただく</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 隣の方から野菜をたくさん頂きました。
example_sentences.english: Our neighbor gave us a whole lot of vegetables.
example_sentences.furigana: 隣[となり]の方[ほう]から野[や]菜[さい]をたくさん頂[いただ]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: お水を少し頂いてもいいですか。
example_sentences.english: Could I have a little water?
example_sentences.furigana: お水[みず]を少[すこ]し頂[いただ]いてもいいですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 駅で親切な女性に地図を頂きました。
example_sentences.english: A kind woman at the station gave me a map.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]で親[しん]切[せつ]な女[じょ]性[せい]に地[ち]図[ず]を頂[いただ]きました。

items.reading_composition: Mixed — 差（さ）on'yomi ＋ し ＋ 上（あ）kun'yomi ＋ げ ＋ る.
items.mnemonic_text: Offering something up respectfully: sashiageru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Noticing the <kanji form="差">difference</kanji> in rank between you and the higher-ranked person, you raise the gift <kanji form="上">up</kanji> with both arms so it travels toward them. Handing something upward across that gap is to <vocabulary form="差し上げる">give, humbly</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: お客さんにお茶を差し上げてください。
example_sentences.english: Please serve our guest some tea.
example_sentences.furigana: お客[きゃく]さんにお茶[ちゃ]を差[さ]し上[あ]げてください。

example_sentences.japanese: 旅館の方に、外国のお菓子を差し上げました。
example_sentences.english: I gave the staff at the inn some sweets from abroad.
example_sentences.furigana: 旅[りょ]館[かん]の方[ほう]に、外[がい]国[こく]のお菓[か]子[し]を差[さ]し上[あ]げました。

example_sentences.japanese: この本、よかったら差し上げます。
example_sentences.english: If you'd like this book, it's yours.
example_sentences.furigana: この本[ほん]、よかったら差[さ]し上[あ]げます。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 下（くだ）＋さる.
items.mnemonic_text: Graciously handing something down: kudasaru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: An honored person hands the gift <kanji form="下">down</kanji> to where you stand, well <kanji form="下">below</kanji> their seat. A present that travels downward from someone that far over you is one they <vocabulary form="下さる">give you, honorifically</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, perches on the power line and drops little glowing medals of <reading>kudos</reading> onto everyone waiting below. A gift handed down from a bird perched that high is <vocabulary form="下さる">to give, honorifically</vocabulary>, landing with the sound <reading>くださる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 医者が新しい薬を下さいました。
example_sentences.english: The doctor gave me a new medicine.
example_sentences.furigana: 医[い]者[しゃ]が新[あたら]しい薬[くすり]を下[くだ]さいました。

example_sentences.japanese: 叔父が古いカメラを下さいました。
example_sentences.english: My uncle gave me his old camera.
example_sentences.furigana: 叔父[おじ]が古[ふる]いカメラを下[くだ]さいました。

example_sentences.japanese: 雨の中、迎えに来て下さって、本当に助かりました。
example_sentences.english: You came to pick me up in the rain, and it really saved me.
example_sentences.furigana: 雨[あめ]の中[なか]、迎[むか]えに来[き]て下[くだ]さって、本[ほん]当[とう]に助[たす]かりました。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 承（しょう）＋知（ち）＋する, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Receiving (承) knowledge (知) humbly: shouchi suru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: An order comes in and lands dead center, the way the arrow thumps into the target: now you <kanji form="知">know</kanji> it. Bowing to show it struck home and you will carry it out is how you <vocabulary form="承知する">acknowledge an instruction, humbly</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: はい、承知しました。書類は明日の朝までに送ります。
example_sentences.english: Yes, understood. I'll send the documents by tomorrow morning.
example_sentences.furigana: はい、承[しょう]知[ち]しました。書[しょ]類[るい]は明日[あした]の朝[あさ]までに送[おく]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: 店員は「承知しました」と言って、すぐ席を準備した。
example_sentences.english: The clerk said "Certainly" and got a seat ready right away.
example_sentences.furigana: 店[てん]員[いん]は「承[しょう]知[ち]しました」と言[い]って、すぐ席[せき]を準[じゅん]備[び]した。

example_sentences.japanese: 値段が高いことは承知していますが、これを買います。
example_sentences.english: I'm well aware it's expensive, but I'll take this one.
example_sentences.furigana: 値[ね]段[だん]が高[たか]いことは承[しょう]知[ち]していますが、これを買[か]います。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 話（はな）＋せる.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of hanasu: able to speak.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Hand the nonstop <kanji form="話">talker</kanji> with the wagging tongue an open microphone and the words just pour out, no gap anywhere. Being able to let language run like that is what it means to <vocabulary form="話せる">be able to speak</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 話 is read 「はな」 from 話す, so <vocabulary form="話せる">can speak</vocabulary> comes out as <reading>はなせる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 弟は英語が少し話せます。
example_sentences.english: My little brother can speak a bit of English.
example_sentences.furigana: 弟[おとうと]は英[えい]語[ご]が少[すこ]し話[はな]せます。

example_sentences.japanese: 風邪で声が出ないので、今日はあまり話せません。
example_sentences.english: I've lost my voice to a cold, so I can't talk much today.
example_sentences.furigana: 風邪[かぜ]で声[こえ]が出[で]ないので、今日[きょう]はあまり話[はな]せません。

example_sentences.japanese: 犬と話せたら、楽しいでしょうね。
example_sentences.english: It would be fun if I could talk with my dog.
example_sentences.furigana: 犬[いぬ]と話[はな]せたら、楽[たの]しいでしょうね。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 書（か）＋ける.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of kaku: able to write.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="書">write</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="書ける">can write</vocabulary> word are the same character, so they mean the same thing. The added ending only shifts it from doing the writing to being able to do it.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 書 is read 「か」 from 書く, so <vocabulary form="書ける">can write</vocabulary> comes out as <reading>かける</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 妹はもうひらがなで自分の名前が書けます。
example_sentences.english: My little sister can already write her own name in hiragana.
example_sentences.furigana: 妹[いもうと]はもうひらがなで自[じ]分[ぶん]の名[な]前[まえ]が書[か]けます。

example_sentences.japanese: このペンは古いですが、まだよく書けますよ。
example_sentences.english: This pen is old, but it still writes well.
example_sentences.furigana: このペンは古[ふる]いですが、まだよく書[か]けますよ。

example_sentences.japanese: チョークがないので、黒板に書けません。
example_sentences.english: There's no chalk, so I can't write on the blackboard.
example_sentences.furigana: チョークがないので、黒[こく]板[ばん]に書[か]けません。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 読（よ）＋める.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of yomu: able to read.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="読">read</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="読める">can read</vocabulary> word are the same character, so they point at the same meaning. The extra ending just moves it from reading to being able to read.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 読 is read 「よ」 from 読む, so <vocabulary form="読める">can read</vocabulary> comes out as <reading>よめる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: この漢字、読めますか。
example_sentences.english: Can you read this kanji?
example_sentences.furigana: この漢[かん]字[じ]、読[よ]めますか。

example_sentences.japanese: 眼鏡がなければ、祖父は新聞が読めません。
example_sentences.english: Without his glasses, my grandfather can't read the newspaper.
example_sentences.furigana: 眼鏡[めがね]がなければ、祖[そ]父[ふ]は新[しん]聞[ぶん]が読[よ]めません。

example_sentences.japanese: 部屋が暗くて、地図がよく読めません。
example_sentences.english: The room is dark, so I can't really read the map.
example_sentences.furigana: 部屋[へや]が暗[くら]くて、地[ち]図[ず]がよく読[よ]めません。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 使（つか）＋える.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of tsukau: usable.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Nothing new happens here: the <kanji form="使">use</kanji> kanji you already know is exactly what <vocabulary form="使える">can use</vocabulary> means.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already met 「つか」 in 使う, so <vocabulary form="使える">can use</vocabulary> just wears that same reading with a new tail: <reading>つかえる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: この店では現金しか使えません。
example_sentences.english: This shop only takes cash.
example_sentences.furigana: この店[みせ]では現[げん]金[きん]しか使[つか]えません。

example_sentences.japanese: 父はパソコンが全然使えません。
example_sentences.english: My dad can't use a computer at all.
example_sentences.furigana: 父[ちち]はパソコンが全[ぜん]然[ぜん]使[つか]えません。

example_sentences.japanese: 冷蔵庫が壊れて使えないので、困っています。
example_sentences.english: The fridge broke and won't work, so I'm stuck.
example_sentences.furigana: 冷[れい]蔵[ぞう]庫[こ]が壊[こわ]れて使[つか]えないので、困[こま]っています。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 行（い）＋ける.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of iku: able to go.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="行">go</kanji> kanji stands on its own here, so <vocabulary form="行ける">can go</vocabulary> is that same kanji and not one idea more.
items.reading_mnemonic: The 「い」 in this word is the one from 行く that you already know, so <vocabulary form="行ける">can go</vocabulary> comes out as <reading>いける</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 駅までは歩いて五分で行けます。
example_sentences.english: You can get to the station in five minutes on foot.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]までは歩[ある]いて五[ご]分[ふん]で行[い]けます。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日は用事があるから、山には行けません。
example_sentences.english: I have something to do tomorrow, so I can't go to the mountains.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]は用[よう]事[じ]があるから、山[やま]には行[い]けません。

example_sentences.japanese: 自転車なら、あの公園まで行けるよ。
example_sentences.english: By bike, you can make it to that park.
example_sentences.furigana: 自[じ]転[てん]車[しゃ]なら、あの公[こう]園[えん]まで行[い]けるよ。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 来（こ）＋られる.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of kuru: able to come.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="来">come</kanji> kanji is the whole of this word, so <vocabulary form="来られる">can come</vocabulary> holds nothing the character did not already carry.
items.reading_mnemonic: As the burst rice grain scatters over the flat ground, the farmer asks his wife <reading>Cora, really?</reading> and she nods: a whole crop <vocabulary form="来られる">can come</vocabulary> up from that, <reading>こられる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 田中さんは来週の会議に来られますか。
example_sentences.english: Can Mr. Tanaka come to next week's meeting?
example_sentences.furigana: 田中[たなか]さんは来[らい]週[しゅう]の会[かい]議[ぎ]に来[こ]られますか。

example_sentences.japanese: 雪が多くて、先生は学校に来られませんでした。
example_sentences.english: There was so much snow that the teacher couldn't make it to school.
example_sentences.furigana: 雪[ゆき]が多[おお]くて、先[せん]生[せい]は学[がっ]校[こう]に来[こ]られませんでした。

example_sentences.japanese: 日曜日なら、うちに来られる？
example_sentences.english: Can you come over to my place on Sunday?
example_sentences.furigana: 日[にち]曜[よう]日[び]なら、うちに来[こ]られる？

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 食（た）＋べられる.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of taberu: able to eat.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="食">eat</kanji> kanji does all the work on its own here, so <vocabulary form="食べられる">can eat</vocabulary> means just what that character has always meant.
items.reading_mnemonic: That 「た」 is the same one 食べる taught you earlier, so <vocabulary form="食べられる">can eat</vocabulary> is simply <reading>たべられる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 息子は辛い料理が食べられません。
example_sentences.english: My son can't eat spicy food.
example_sentences.furigana: 息子[むすこ]は辛[から]い料[りょう]理[り]が食[た]べられません。

example_sentences.japanese: この花は食べられるんですか。
example_sentences.english: Wait, you can eat this flower?
example_sentences.furigana: この花[はな]は食[た]べられるんですか。

example_sentences.japanese: お腹が痛くて、昼ご飯が半分しか食べられなかった。
example_sentences.english: My stomach hurt, so I could only eat half my lunch.
example_sentences.furigana: お腹[なか]が痛[いた]くて、昼[ひる]ご飯[はん]が半[はん]分[ぶん]しか食[た]べられなかった。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 飲（の）＋める.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of nomu: able to drink.
items.meaning_mnemonic: No story to build here: the <kanji form="飲">drink</kanji> kanji is the whole word, and <vocabulary form="飲める">can drink</vocabulary> means the very same thing.
items.reading_mnemonic: You know 「の」 already from 飲む, so <vocabulary form="飲める">can drink</vocabulary> follows straight on as <reading>のめる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: このお茶は熱すぎて、まだ飲めません。
example_sentences.english: This tea is too hot to drink yet.
example_sentences.furigana: このお茶[ちゃ]は熱[ねつ]すぎて、まだ飲[の]めません。

example_sentences.japanese: 夫はお酒があまり飲めません。
example_sentences.english: My husband can't drink much alcohol.
example_sentences.furigana: 夫[おっと]はお酒[さけ]があまり飲[の]めません。

example_sentences.japanese: この薬はご飯の前に飲めますか。
example_sentences.english: Can I take this medicine before meals?
example_sentences.furigana: この薬[くすり]はご飯[はん]の前[まえ]に飲[の]めますか。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 見（み）＋られる.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of miru: able to see.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="見">see</kanji> kanji does not change when it becomes a word, so <vocabulary form="見られる">can see</vocabulary> is simply the character you have already met.
items.reading_mnemonic: This 「み」 is the reading you picked up in 見る, so <vocabulary form="見られる">can see</vocabulary> comes out as <reading>みられる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: このホテルの部屋から海が見られます。
example_sentences.english: You can see the sea from this hotel room.
example_sentences.furigana: このホテルの部屋[へや]から海[うみ]が見[み]られます。

example_sentences.japanese: 仕事が忙しくて、映画が見られなかった。
example_sentences.english: Work was so busy that I couldn't see the movie.
example_sentences.furigana: 仕[し]事[ごと]が忙[いそが]しくて、映[えい]画[が]が見[み]られなかった。

example_sentences.japanese: 夏の夜は、湖の上にたくさんの星が見られます。
example_sentences.english: On summer nights, you can see lots of stars over the lake.
example_sentences.furigana: 夏[なつ]の夜[よる]は、湖[みずうみ]の上[うえ]にたくさんの星[ほし]が見[み]られます。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 出（で）＋来（き）＋る.
items.mnemonic_text: Kanji form of dekiru: to be possible.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Once every part has <kanji form="来">come</kanji> in, a finished thing <kanji form="出">exits</kanji> the far end of the line. That finished thing is proof the whole job was <vocabulary form="出来る">possible</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: この仕事は一人で出来ますか。
example_sentences.english: Can you handle this job on your own?
example_sentences.furigana: この仕[し]事[ごと]は一人[ひとり]で出[で]来[き]ますか。

example_sentences.japanese: 図書館の中では電話が出来ません。
example_sentences.english: You can't make phone calls inside the library.
example_sentences.furigana: 図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]の中[なか]では電[でん]話[わ]が出[で]来[き]ません。

example_sentences.japanese: 姉は英語と日本語が出来ます。
example_sentences.english: My older sister can speak English and Japanese.
example_sentences.furigana: 姉[あね]は英[えい]語[ご]と日本[にほん]語[ご]が出[で]来[き]ます。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 泳（およ）＋げる.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of oyogu: able to swim.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Step off the riverbank into deep water and you do not go under; your limbs already know the strokes. Holding yourself up and moving through the water on your own is what it means that you <vocabulary form="泳げる">can swim</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 「およ」 from 泳ぐ, so <vocabulary form="泳げる">can swim</vocabulary> simply becomes <reading>およげる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 犬は泳げますが、うちの猫は泳げません。
example_sentences.english: Dogs can swim, but our cat can't.
example_sentences.furigana: 犬[いぬ]は泳[およ]げますが、うちの猫[ねこ]は泳[およ]げません。

example_sentences.japanese: この川は浅いから、子供でも泳げます。
example_sentences.english: This river is shallow, so even kids can swim in it.
example_sentences.furigana: この川[かわ]は浅[あさ]いから、子[こ]供[ども]でも泳[およ]げます。

example_sentences.japanese: 娘は去年から泳げるようになりました。
example_sentences.english: My daughter learned to swim last year.
example_sentences.furigana: 娘[むすめ]は去[きょ]年[ねん]から泳[およ]げるようになりました。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 走（はし）＋れる.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of hashiru: able to run.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Same character, same meaning: the <kanji form="走">run</kanji> kanji you already know is all there is to <vocabulary form="走れる">can run</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The 「はし」 here is the same one from 走る, so <vocabulary form="走れる">can run</vocabulary> reads as <reading>はしれる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 足が痛くて、今日は走れません。
example_sentences.english: My leg hurts, so I can't run today.
example_sentences.furigana: 足[あし]が痛[いた]くて、今日[きょう]は走[はし]れません。

example_sentences.japanese: 祖父は八十歳ですが、まだ速く走れます。
example_sentences.english: My grandfather is eighty, but he can still run fast.
example_sentences.furigana: 祖[そ]父[ふ]は八[はち]十[じゅう]歳[さい]ですが、まだ速[はや]く走[はし]れます。

example_sentences.japanese: この靴なら、雨の道でも走れるよ。
example_sentences.english: In these shoes, you can run even on a wet road.
example_sentences.furigana: この靴[くつ]なら、雨[あめ]の道[みち]でも走[はし]れるよ。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 会（あ）＋える.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of au: able to meet.
items.meaning_mnemonic: There is nothing extra to learn here, since the <kanji form="会">meet</kanji> kanji and the word <vocabulary form="会える">can meet</vocabulary> point at exactly the same idea.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already say 「あ」 this way in 会う, so <vocabulary form="会える">can meet</vocabulary> is nothing more than <reading>あえる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 来月、外国に住んでいる姉に会えます。
example_sentences.english: Next month I get to see my sister who lives abroad.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]月[げつ]、外[がい]国[こく]に住[す]んでいる姉[あね]に会[あ]えます。

example_sentences.japanese: 忙しくて、恋人に全然会えない。
example_sentences.english: I'm so busy I never get to see my partner.
example_sentences.furigana: 忙[いそが]しくて、恋[こい]人[びと]に全[ぜん]然[ぜん]会[あ]えない。

example_sentences.japanese: 駅の出口で待っていれば、すぐ会えるでしょう。
example_sentences.english: If you wait at the station exit, you'll find each other right away.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]の出[で]口[ぐち]で待[ま]っていれば、すぐ会[あ]えるでしょう。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 買（か）＋える.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of kau: able to buy.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="買">buy</kanji> kanji carries straight over into this word, so <vocabulary form="買える">can buy</vocabulary> holds no meaning the kanji did not already.
items.reading_mnemonic: That 「か」 is the reading 買う already gave you, so <vocabulary form="買える">can buy</vocabulary> lands as <reading>かえる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 切手はコンビニでも買えますよ。
example_sentences.english: You can buy stamps at a convenience store too.
example_sentences.furigana: 切[きっ]手[て]はコンビニでも買[か]えますよ。

example_sentences.japanese: 千円で、弁当が二つ買えました。
example_sentences.english: I was able to buy two boxed lunches for a thousand yen.
example_sentences.furigana: 千[せん]円[えん]で、弁[べん]当[とう]が二[ふた]つ買[か]えました。

example_sentences.japanese: 値段が高すぎて、あの時計は買えなかった。
example_sentences.english: That watch was way too expensive, so I couldn't buy it.
example_sentences.furigana: 値[ね]段[だん]が高[たか]すぎて、あの時計[とけい]は買[か]えなかった。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 乗（の）＋れる.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of noru: able to ride.
items.meaning_mnemonic: This word adds nothing to its kanji: <vocabulary form="乗れる">can ride</vocabulary> is the <kanji form="乗">ride</kanji> kanji you have already met, unchanged.
items.reading_mnemonic: The 「の」 in this word comes straight from 乗る, so <vocabulary form="乗れる">can ride</vocabulary> simply becomes <reading>のれる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 妹は六歳で自転車に乗れるようになった。
example_sentences.english: My little sister learned to ride a bike at six.
example_sentences.furigana: 妹[いもうと]は六[ろく]歳[さい]で自[じ]転[てん]車[しゃ]に乗[の]れるようになった。

example_sentences.japanese: 荷物が多くて、バスに乗れませんでした。
example_sentences.english: I had too much luggage to get on the bus.
example_sentences.furigana: 荷[に]物[もつ]が多[おお]くて、バスに乗[の]れませんでした。

example_sentences.japanese: この車は七人乗れます。
example_sentences.english: This car seats seven people.
example_sentences.furigana: この車[くるま]は七[なな]人[にん]乗[の]れます。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 行（い）＋かせる.
items.mnemonic_text: The causative of iku: making someone go.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At its core this word is still the <kanji form="行">go</kanji> kanji. The tail added on means you <vocabulary form="行かせる">make or let someone go</vocabulary>, whether they want to or not.
items.reading_mnemonic: Same 「い」 as in 行く, so <vocabulary form="行かせる">to make/let go</vocabulary> keeps that opening sound and becomes <reading>いかせる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 雨が強いので、子供を一人で学校に行かせたくない。
example_sentences.english: The rain is heavy, so I don't want to let my kid go to school alone.
example_sentences.furigana: 雨[あめ]が強[つよ]いので、子[こ]供[ども]を一人[ひとり]で学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]かせたくない。

example_sentences.japanese: 会社は来年、夫を外国の工場に行かせるそうです。
example_sentences.english: I hear the company is sending my husband to a factory abroad next year.
example_sentences.furigana: 会[かい]社[しゃ]は来[らい]年[ねん]、夫[おっと]を外[がい]国[こく]の工[こう]場[じょう]に行[い]かせるそうです。

example_sentences.japanese: 気分が悪いなら、娘を病院に行かせましょう。
example_sentences.english: If she feels sick, let's send our daughter to the hospital.
example_sentences.furigana: 気[き]分[ぶん]が悪[わる]いなら、娘[むすめ]を病[びょう]院[いん]に行[い]かせましょう。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 食（た）＋べさせる.
items.mnemonic_text: The causative of taberu: making someone eat.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Underneath, this is only the <kanji form="食">eat</kanji> kanji again. The extra endings shift it to mean you <vocabulary form="食べさせる">make or let another person eat</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The 「た」 is the one 食べる gave you, so <vocabulary form="食べさせる">to make/let eat</vocabulary> starts the same and runs on to <reading>たべさせる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 母は毎朝、弟に野菜を食べさせます。
example_sentences.english: Every morning, my mother makes my little brother eat vegetables.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]、弟[おとうと]に野[や]菜[さい]を食[た]べさせます。

example_sentences.japanese: 猫に人の食べ物を食べさせないでください。
example_sentences.english: Please don't feed the cat people food.
example_sentences.furigana: 猫[ねこ]に人[ひと]の食[た]べ物[もの]を食[た]べさせないでください。

example_sentences.japanese: 赤ちゃんにスプーンでご飯を食べさせた。
example_sentences.english: I fed the baby rice with a spoon.
example_sentences.furigana: 赤[あか]ちゃんにスプーンでご飯[はん]を食[た]べさせた。

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: The causative of yaru: making someone do it.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Run a <reading>yard sale</reading> and you get one afternoon to <vocabulary form="やらせる">make or let someone else do</vocabulary> every bit of the lifting and pricing. Handing the whole driveway to other hands like that is <reading>やらせる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 先生は生徒に同じ問題を三回やらせた。
example_sentences.english: The teacher made the students do the same problem three times.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]は生[せい]徒[と]に同[おな]じ問[もん]題[だい]を三[さん]回[かい]やらせた。

example_sentences.japanese: 難しい仕事ですが、新しい店員にやらせることにしました。
example_sentences.english: It's a hard job, but I've decided to let the new clerk do it.
example_sentences.furigana: 難[むずか]しい仕[し]事[ごと]ですが、新[あたら]しい店[てん]員[いん]にやらせることにしました。

example_sentences.japanese: 兄は自分の宿題をいつも僕にやらせる。
example_sentences.english: My big brother always makes me do his homework.
example_sentences.furigana: 兄[あに]は自[じ]分[ぶん]の宿[しゅく]題[だい]をいつも僕[ぼく]にやらせる。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 待（ま）＋たされる.
items.mnemonic_text: The causative-passive of matsu: being kept waiting.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="待">wait</kanji> kanji sits at the centre of this word unchanged. The endings stacked after it turn plain waiting into <vocabulary form="待たされる">being made to wait</vocabulary> by someone who will not hurry.
items.reading_mnemonic: You learned 「ま」 back in 待つ, so the drawn-out <vocabulary form="待たされる">to be made to wait</vocabulary> is still just <reading>またされる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 銀行の窓口で一時間も待たされた。
example_sentences.english: I was kept waiting a whole hour at the bank counter.
example_sentences.furigana: 銀[ぎん]行[こう]の窓[まど]口[ぐち]で一[いち]時[じ]間[かん]も待[ま]たされた。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は約束に遅れるから、私はよく待たされる。
example_sentences.english: She's always late for our plans, so I often end up waiting.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は約[やく]束[そく]に遅[おく]れるから、私[わたし]はよく待[ま]たされる。

example_sentences.japanese: 雪で電車が止まって、寒い外で待たされた。
example_sentences.english: The snow stopped the trains, and we were left waiting out in the cold.
example_sentences.furigana: 雪[ゆき]で電[でん]車[しゃ]が止[と]まって、寒[さむ]い外[そと]で待[ま]たされた。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 叱（しか）＋られる.
items.mnemonic_text: The passive of shikaru: on the receiving end of a scolding.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Knock a jar off Grandma Kane's shelf and every cat goes still while she turns and scolds you in a long, rising voice. Standing there and taking all of it is what it means <vocabulary form="叱られる">to be scolded</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 「しか」 from 叱る, so the version done to you, <vocabulary form="叱られる">to be scolded</vocabulary>, is <reading>しかられる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 夜遅く帰ったら、父に叱られた。
example_sentences.english: I got home late at night and got scolded by my dad.
example_sentences.furigana: 夜[よる]遅[おそ]く帰[かえ]ったら、父[ちち]に叱[しか]られた。

example_sentences.japanese: 図書館で大きい声で話して、叱られました。
example_sentences.english: I talked loudly in the library and got told off.
example_sentences.furigana: 図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]で大[おお]きい声[こえ]で話[はな]して、叱[しか]られました。

example_sentences.japanese: 犬がテーブルの肉を食べて、叱られている。
example_sentences.english: The dog ate the meat off the table and is getting scolded.
example_sentences.furigana: 犬[いぬ]がテーブルの肉[にく]を食[た]べて、叱[しか]られている。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 褒（ほ）＋められる.
items.mnemonic_text: The passive of homeru: receiving praise.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Hand a drawing to the teacher and she holds it up to the whole class, naming every good line in it. Having your work lifted up for the whole room to see is what it means <vocabulary form="褒められる">to be praised</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 「ほ」 from 褒める, so the same thing coming back at you, <vocabulary form="褒められる">to be praised</vocabulary>, is <reading>ほめられる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 料理が上手だと、祖母に褒められた。
example_sentences.english: My grandmother praised me for being a good cook.
example_sentences.furigana: 料[りょう]理[り]が上手[じょうず]だと、祖[そ]母[ぼ]に褒[ほ]められた。

example_sentences.japanese: 褒められたら、誰でも嬉しいです。
example_sentences.english: Anyone is happy when they're praised.
example_sentences.furigana: 褒[ほ]められたら、誰[だれ]でも嬉[うれ]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 私の絵が美術の授業で褒められた。
example_sentences.english: My painting got praised in art class.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の絵[え]が美[び]術[じゅつ]の授[じゅ]業[ぎょう]で褒[ほ]められた。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 泣（な）＋かれる.
items.mnemonic_text: The passive of naku: suffering from someone's crying.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The person beside you suddenly bursts out <kanji form="泣">crying</kanji>, and now their misery is your problem to deal with. Being left holding someone else's tears like that is being <vocabulary form="泣かれる">cried at</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 「な」 from 泣く, so that same crying aimed at you, <vocabulary form="泣かれる">to be cried at (adversity)</vocabulary>, is <reading>なかれる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 電車の中で赤ちゃんに泣かれて、困りました。
example_sentences.english: A baby started crying right next to me on the train, and I didn't know what to do.
example_sentences.furigana: 電[でん]車[しゃ]の中[なか]で赤[あか]ちゃんに泣[な]かれて、困[こま]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: 妹に泣かれたので、お菓子を半分あげました。
example_sentences.english: My little sister burst into tears, so I gave her half my snacks.
example_sentences.furigana: 妹[いもうと]に泣[な]かれたので、お菓[か]子[し]を半[はん]分[ぶん]あげました。

example_sentences.japanese: 空港で母に泣かれて、少し恥ずかしかったです。
example_sentences.english: My mom cried at the airport, and I was a little embarrassed.
example_sentences.furigana: 空[くう]港[こう]で母[はは]に泣[な]かれて、少[すこ]し恥[は]ずかしかったです。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 殺（ころ）＋す.
items.mnemonic_text: A blow (殳) striking down: to kill.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Yank the wrong lever on the old mower and the motor goes quiet for good under your hands. Ending a running thing on purpose like that is what it means <vocabulary form="殺す">to kill</vocabulary> it.
items.reading_mnemonic: Yank the wrong lever on the old mower in the middle of its roaring <reading>chorus</reading>, and the motor goes quiet under your hands for good: <reading>ころす</reading>, to <vocabulary form="殺す">kill</vocabulary> it.

example_sentences.japanese: 図書館で声を殺して笑いました。
example_sentences.english: I laughed in the library, trying not to make a sound.
example_sentences.furigana: 図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]で声[こえ]を殺[ころ]して笑[わら]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 部屋の蚊を殺すまで、寝ることができなかった。
example_sentences.english: I couldn't sleep until I'd killed the mosquito in my room.
example_sentences.furigana: 部屋[へや]の蚊[か]を殺[ころ]すまで、寝[ね]ることができなかった。

example_sentences.japanese: 祖父は「動物を殺してはいけない」とよく言っていました。
example_sentences.english: My grandfather often said you must never kill animals.
example_sentences.furigana: 祖[そ]父[ふ]は「動[どう]物[ぶつ]を殺[ころ]してはいけない」とよく言[い]っていました。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 殺（ころ）＋される.
items.mnemonic_text: The passive of korosu: to be killed.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A beetle wanders onto the train track at exactly the wrong second. The 8:15 does not slow down, and being the one it happens to is <vocabulary form="殺される">to be killed</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 殺 is 「ころ」 from 殺す, the verb you first met it in, so <vocabulary form="殺される">to be killed</vocabulary> is <reading>ころされる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日見た映画では、最初に医者が殺されました。
example_sentences.english: In the movie I saw yesterday, the doctor is the first one killed.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]見[み]た映[えい]画[が]では、最[さい]初[しょ]に医[い]者[しゃ]が殺[ころ]されました。

example_sentences.japanese: 兄のカメラを壊したので、殺されるかもしれません。
example_sentences.english: I broke my brother's camera, so he might just kill me.
example_sentences.furigana: 兄[あに]のカメラを壊[こわ]したので、殺[ころ]されるかもしれません。

example_sentences.japanese: その男の人は殺されたと警官が言いました。
example_sentences.english: The police officer said the man had been killed.
example_sentences.furigana: その男[おとこ]の人[ひと]は殺[ころ]されたと警[けい]官[かん]が言[い]いました。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 出（で）＋かける.
items.mnemonic_text: Exiting (出) and setting off: dekakeru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Climbing out over the box rim is only the <kanji form="出">exit</kanji>. Once your feet hit the road and you keep walking, that is <vocabulary form="出かける">to go out / head out</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 出 is 「で」 from 出る, the verb it first showed up in, so <vocabulary form="出かける">to go out / head out</vocabulary> is <reading>でかける</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 日曜日は雨だったので、どこにも出かけませんでした。
example_sentences.english: It rained on Sunday, so I didn't go out anywhere.
example_sentences.furigana: 日[にち]曜[よう]日[び]は雨[あめ]だったので、どこにも出[で]かけませんでした。

example_sentences.japanese: 祖母は毎朝、近くの公園へ出かけます。
example_sentences.english: Every morning my grandmother heads out to the park nearby.
example_sentences.furigana: 祖[そ]母[ぼ]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]、近[ちか]くの公[こう]園[えん]へ出[で]かけます。

example_sentences.japanese: 出かける前に、窓を閉めてください。
example_sentences.english: Please close the windows before you head out.
example_sentences.furigana: 出[で]かける前[まえ]に、窓[まど]を閉[し]めてください。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 取（と）＋り＋替（か）＋える.
items.mnemonic_text: Taking (取り) and changing (替える): to swap.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="取">take</kanji> the worn part out by the ear, the rude fast way, and drop a fresh one into the gap it left. Swapping the old for the new like that is <vocabulary form="取り替える">to exchange / replace</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 台所の電気が暗くなったので、新しいのに取り替えました。
example_sentences.english: The kitchen light had gotten dim, so I replaced it with a new one.
example_sentences.furigana: 台[だい]所[どころ]の電[でん]気[き]が暗[くら]くなったので、新[あたら]しいのに取[と]り替[か]えました。

example_sentences.japanese: このシャツは小さすぎたので、店で大きいのと取り替えてもらいました。
example_sentences.english: This shirt was too small, so the shop swapped it for a bigger one.
example_sentences.furigana: このシャツは小[ちい]さすぎたので、店[みせ]で大[おお]きいのと取[と]り替[か]えてもらいました。

example_sentences.japanese: 汚いタオルは毎日取り替えるようにしています。
example_sentences.english: I make a point of changing out dirty towels every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 汚[きたな]いタオルは毎[まい]日[にち]取[と]り替[か]えるようにしています。

items.word_type: godan verb, transitive verb, intransitive verb
items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 繰（く）＋り＋返（かえ）＋す.
items.mnemonic_text: Reeling (繰り) something back (返す): to repeat.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You set the reel <kanji form="繰">winding</kanji> forward, it <kanji form="返">return</kanji>s to the very same mark, and your hand starts it winding again. Motion that keeps coming back to its start is <vocabulary form="繰り返す">to repeat</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 先生は同じ質問をもう一度繰り返しました。
example_sentences.english: The teacher repeated the same question one more time.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]は同[おな]じ質[しつ]問[もん]をもう一[いち]度[ど]繰[く]り返[かえ]しました。

example_sentences.japanese: 弟はテレビで聞いた歌を何回も繰り返して歌っています。
example_sentences.english: My little brother keeps singing a song he heard on TV, over and over.
example_sentences.furigana: 弟[おとうと]はテレビで聞[き]いた歌[うた]を何[なん]回[かい]も繰[く]り返[かえ]して歌[うた]っています。

example_sentences.japanese: 覚えるまで、声に出して繰り返しましょう。
example_sentences.english: Let's say it out loud again and again until it sticks.
example_sentences.furigana: 覚[おぼ]えるまで、声[こえ]に出[だ]して繰[く]り返[かえ]しましょう。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 取（と）＋り＋掛（か）＋かる.
items.mnemonic_text: Taking (取り) hold (掛かる) of a task: to begin work.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You get a grip on the job and <kanji form="掛">hang</kanji> your whole weight from it, the rude fast way you would <kanji form="取">take</kanji> hold of someone by the ear. Latching on and leaning in like that is <vocabulary form="取り掛かる">to set about (a task)</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 晩ご飯の後で、すぐ宿題に取り掛かりました。
example_sentences.english: Right after dinner, I got straight to work on my homework.
example_sentences.furigana: 晩[ばん]ご飯[はん]の後[あと]で、すぐ宿[しゅく]題[だい]に取[と]り掛[か]かりました。

example_sentences.japanese: 来週から新しい本に取り掛かるつもりです。
example_sentences.english: I'm planning to start on a new book next week.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]週[しゅう]から新[あたら]しい本[ほん]に取[と]り掛[か]かるつもりです。

example_sentences.japanese: お客さんが来るので、夫は午後から料理に取り掛かりました。
example_sentences.english: Guests were coming, so my husband started on the cooking in the afternoon.
example_sentences.furigana: お客[きゃく]さんが来[く]るので、夫[おっと]は午[ご]後[ご]から料[りょう]理[り]に取[と]り掛[か]かりました。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 持（も）＋ち＋帰（かえ）＋る.
items.mnemonic_text: Holding (持ち) and returning (帰る): to take away.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji form="持">hold</kanji> on the warm food box never loosens the whole walk home, right up to the moment you <kanji form="帰">return</kanji> through your own door. Carrying your meal back that way is <vocabulary form="持ち帰る">to take home / take out</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 残った食べ物を持ち帰ってもいいですか。
example_sentences.english: Is it okay if I take the leftover food home?
example_sentences.furigana: 残[のこ]った食[た]べ物[もの]を持[も]ち帰[かえ]ってもいいですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 仕事は家に持ち帰らないようにしています。
example_sentences.english: I try not to bring work home.
example_sentences.furigana: 仕[し]事[ごと]は家[いえ]に持[も]ち帰[かえ]らないようにしています。

example_sentences.japanese: 山で使った物は、全部持ち帰りましょう。
example_sentences.english: Let's take everything we used on the mountain back home with us.
example_sentences.furigana: 山[やま]で使[つか]った物[もの]は、全[ぜん]部[ぶ]持[も]ち帰[かえ]りましょう。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 連（つ）＋れて＋行（い）＋く.
items.mnemonic_text: Bringing (連れて) someone along as you go (行く).
items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="行">go</kanji> off down the crossroads with your little brother gripped by the sleeve so he cannot peel away. Setting out with a person fastened to your side like that is <vocabulary form="連れて行く">to take (a person) along</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 夏になったら、娘を海へ連れて行くと約束しました。
example_sentences.english: I promised my daughter I'd take her to the sea when summer comes.
example_sentences.furigana: 夏[なつ]になったら、娘[むすめ]を海[うみ]へ連[つ]れて行[い]くと約[やく]束[そく]しました。

example_sentences.japanese: 犬を店の中に連れて行くことはできません。
example_sentences.english: You can't take dogs inside the shop.
example_sentences.furigana: 犬[いぬ]を店[みせ]の中[なか]に連[つ]れて行[い]くことはできません。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達を駅の近くのいい喫茶店に連れて行くことにしました。
example_sentences.english: I've decided to take my friend to a nice coffee shop near the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]を駅[えき]の近[ちか]くのいい喫[きっ]茶[さ]店[てん]に連[つ]れて行[い]くことにしました。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 連（つ）＋れて＋来（く）＋る.
items.mnemonic_text: Bringing (連れて) someone as you come (来る).
items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="連">lead</kanji> a nervous friend up the path by the hand as the two of you <kanji form="来">come</kanji> toward the house. Turning up with an extra person beside you is <vocabulary form="連れて来る">to bring (a person)</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 息子が恋人を家に連れて来ることになりました。
example_sentences.english: It turns out my son is bringing his girlfriend home.
example_sentences.furigana: 息子[むすこ]が恋[こい]人[びと]を家[いえ]に連[つ]れて来[く]ることになりました。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日の会議に、他の会社の人を連れて来るつもりです。
example_sentences.english: I'm planning to bring someone from another company to tomorrow's meeting.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]の会[かい]議[ぎ]に、他[ほか]の会[かい]社[しゃ]の人[ひと]を連[つ]れて来[く]るつもりです。

example_sentences.japanese: 隣の猫は、よく小さい猫を三匹連れて来る。
example_sentences.english: The neighbor's cat often shows up trailing three little kittens.
example_sentences.furigana: 隣[となり]の猫[ねこ]は、よく小[ちい]さい猫[ねこ]を三[さん]匹[ひき]連[つ]れて来[く]る。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 持（も）＋って＋来（く）＋る.
items.mnemonic_text: Holding (持って) something as you come (来る).
items.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji form="持">hold</kanji> stays locked around the umbrella as you <kanji form="来">come</kanji> back in through the door. Arriving with the thing still in your hand is <vocabulary form="持って来る">to bring (a thing)</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 明日の授業に、自分のパソコンを持って来てください。
example_sentences.english: Please bring your own computer to tomorrow's class.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]の授[じゅ]業[ぎょう]に、自[じ]分[ぶん]のパソコンを持[も]って来[き]てください。

example_sentences.japanese: 兄が台所から冷たい水を持って来てくれました。
example_sentences.english: My older brother brought me cold water from the kitchen.
example_sentences.furigana: 兄[あに]が台[だい]所[どころ]から冷[つめ]たい水[みず]を持[も]って来[き]てくれました。

example_sentences.japanese: 猫が庭から小さい花を持って来ました。
example_sentences.english: The cat brought a small flower in from the garden.
example_sentences.furigana: 猫[ねこ]が庭[にわ]から小[ちい]さい花[はな]を持[も]って来[き]ました。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 持（も）＋って＋行（い）＋く.
items.mnemonic_text: Holding (持って) something as you go (行く).
items.meaning_mnemonic: You clamp your <kanji form="持">hold</kanji> around the lunchbox and <kanji form="行">go</kanji> straight out through the crossroads with it. Carrying the thing away from the house is <vocabulary form="持って行く">to take (a thing)</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 週末、祖父の家へ果物を持って行くつもりです。
example_sentences.english: This weekend I plan to take some fruit to my grandfather's house.
example_sentences.furigana: 週[しゅう]末[まつ]、祖[そ]父[ふ]の家[いえ]へ果物[くだもの]を持[も]って行[い]くつもりです。

example_sentences.japanese: 図書館に辞書を持って行ってもいいですか。
example_sentences.english: Is it okay to take a dictionary into the library?
example_sentences.furigana: 図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]に辞[じ]書[しょ]を持[も]って行[い]ってもいいですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 旅行には軽いかばんを持って行ったほうがいいですよ。
example_sentences.english: You'd better take a light bag on the trip.
example_sentences.furigana: 旅[りょ]行[こう]には軽[かる]いかばんを持[も]って行[い]ったほうがいいですよ。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 話（はな）＋し＋合（あ）＋う.
items.mnemonic_text: Talking (話し) together (合う): to discuss.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Each side <kanji form="話">talk</kanji>s, story after story, until the two accounts finally <kanji form="合">fit</kanji> together. Talk that both sides work at until it matches is <vocabulary form="話し合う">to discuss / talk over</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 夫と来年の旅行の予定を話し合いました。
example_sentences.english: My husband and I talked over our plans for next year's trip.
example_sentences.furigana: 夫[おっと]と来[らい]年[ねん]の旅[りょ]行[こう]の予[よ]定[てい]を話[はな]し合[あ]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 兄弟で、親にあげる物を話し合っています。
example_sentences.english: The siblings are discussing what to give their parents.
example_sentences.furigana: 兄[きょう]弟[だい]で、親[おや]にあげる物[もの]を話[はな]し合[あ]っています。

example_sentences.japanese: 困ったことがあったら、家族でよく話し合いましょう。
example_sentences.english: When something's wrong, let's talk it through properly as a family.
example_sentences.furigana: 困[こま]ったことがあったら、家[か]族[ぞく]でよく話[はな]し合[あ]いましょう。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 見（み）＋送（おく）＋る.
items.mnemonic_text: Watching (見) someone off (送る): to see off.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You keep your <kanji form="見">see</kanji>ing eye locked on your friend while the platform <kanji form="送">send</kanji>s her off down a track you may not follow. Watching a person go until she is out of sight is <vocabulary form="見送る">to see off</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 空港で娘を見送ったとき、少し泣いてしまいました。
example_sentences.english: When I saw my daughter off at the airport, I cried a little.
example_sentences.furigana: 空[くう]港[こう]で娘[むすめ]を見送[みおく]ったとき、少[すこ]し泣[な]いてしまいました。

example_sentences.japanese: お客さんが帰るときは、外まで出て見送りましょう。
example_sentences.english: When guests leave, let's go outside and see them off.
example_sentences.furigana: お客[きゃく]さんが帰[かえ]るときは、外[そと]まで出[で]て見[み]送[おく]りましょう。

example_sentences.japanese: 犬は毎朝、窓から祖母を見送ります。
example_sentences.english: Every morning the dog watches Grandma leave from the window.
example_sentences.furigana: 犬[いぬ]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]、窓[まど]から祖[そ]母[ぼ]を見[み]送[おく]ります。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 見（み）＋回（まわ）＋す.
items.mnemonic_text: Turning (回す) one's view (見): to look around.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji form="見">see</kanji>ing eye travels one full <kanji form="回">round</kanji> of the room, past every wall and back to where it started. Sweeping your gaze in a circle like that is <vocabulary form="見回す">to look around</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 電車を降りてから、駅の中を見回しました。
example_sentences.english: After getting off the train, I looked around the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 電[でん]車[しゃ]を降[お]りてから、駅[えき]の中[なか]を見回[みまわ]しました。

example_sentences.japanese: 弟は知らない町で、不安そうに見回していました。
example_sentences.english: In the unfamiliar town, my little brother was looking around nervously.
example_sentences.furigana: 弟[おとうと]は知[し]らない町[まち]で、不[ふ]安[あん]そうに見回[みまわ]していました。

example_sentences.japanese: 教室を見回したが、先生はまだ来ていなかった。
example_sentences.english: I looked around the classroom, but the teacher hadn't come yet.
example_sentences.furigana: 教[きょう]室[しつ]を見回[みまわ]したが、先[せん]生[せい]はまだ来[き]ていなかった。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 見（み）＋つけ＋出（だ）＋す.
items.mnemonic_text: Finding (見つけ) something and drawing it out (出す).
items.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji form="見">see</kanji>ing eye catches the hidden thing, and you haul it up over the box rim until it <kanji form="出">exit</kanji>s into daylight. Dragging a buried fact into the open is <vocabulary form="見つけ出す">to discover / find out</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 警官は、無くなった自転車を二日で見つけ出しました。
example_sentences.english: The police officer tracked down the missing bicycle in two days.
example_sentences.furigana: 警[けい]官[かん]は、無[な]くなった自[じ]転[てん]車[しゃ]を二日[ふつか]で見[み]つけ出[だ]しました。

example_sentences.japanese: 古い地図で、叔母が生まれた場所を見つけ出した。
example_sentences.english: I found the place where my aunt was born on an old map.
example_sentences.furigana: 古[ふる]い地[ち]図[ず]で、叔母[おば]が生[う]まれた場[ば]所[しょ]を見[み]つけ出[だ]した。

example_sentences.japanese: 妹は、たくさんの写真の中から自分の顔を見つけ出した。
example_sentences.english: My little sister picked out her own face from among lots of photos.
example_sentences.furigana: 妹[いもうと]は、たくさんの写[しゃ]真[しん]の中[なか]から自[じ]分[ぶん]の顔[かお]を見[み]つけ出[だ]した。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 考（かんが）＋え＋出（だ）＋す.
items.mnemonic_text: Thinking (考え) something into being (出す): to devise.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="考">think</kanji>, tracing one old thought down its kinked track until a new idea works loose. Forcing that idea to <kanji form="出">exit</kanji> into the open is <vocabulary form="考え出す">to think up / devise</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 息子は、朝早く起きない理由をいろいろ考え出す。
example_sentences.english: My son thinks up all sorts of reasons not to get up early in the morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 息子[むすこ]は、朝[あさ]早[はや]く起[お]きない理[り]由[ゆう]をいろいろ考[かんが]え出[だ]す。

example_sentences.japanese: この料理は、叔父が考え出したものです。
example_sentences.english: This dish is one my uncle came up with.
example_sentences.furigana: この料[りょう]理[り]は、叔父[おじ]が考[かんが]え出[だ]したものです。

example_sentences.japanese: 会社のみんなで、新しい名前を考え出しました。
example_sentences.english: Everyone at the company came up with a new name together.
example_sentences.furigana: 会[かい]社[しゃ]のみんなで、新[あたら]しい名[な]前[まえ]を考[かんが]え出[だ]しました。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — やり＋直（なお）＋す.
items.mnemonic_text: Doing (やり) it fixed again (直す): to redo.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The moment the work goes wrong, you <kanji form="直">straightaway</kanji> tear it down and carry the pieces back to step one. Building it again from the start like that is <vocabulary form="やり直す">to redo / start over</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 直 is 「なお」 from 直す, the verb it first appeared in, so <vocabulary form="やり直す">to redo / start over</vocabulary> is <reading>やりなおす</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 数学の問題を間違えたので、最初からやり直しました。
example_sentences.english: I got the math problem wrong, so I redid it from the start.
example_sentences.furigana: 数[すう]学[がく]の問[もん]題[だい]を間[ま]違[ちが]えたので、最[さい]初[しょ]からやり直[なお]しました。

example_sentences.japanese: 部屋がまだ汚いと言われて、少年は掃除をやり直した。
example_sentences.english: Told his room was still dirty, the boy did the cleaning over again.
example_sentences.furigana: 部屋[へや]がまだ汚[きたな]いと言[い]われて、少[しょう]年[ねん]は掃[そう]除[じ]をやり直[なお]した。

example_sentences.japanese: 大丈夫、何度でもやり直せますよ。
example_sentences.english: It's fine — you can start over as many times as you like.
example_sentences.furigana: 大[だい]丈[じょう]夫[ぶ]、何[なん]度[ど]でもやり直[なお]せますよ。

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Doing a favor and giving it: yatte ageru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Out on the <reading>yacht, a giraffe</reading> leans up and knots the top sail no sailor can reach, doing it for the whole crew. Doing the work so that someone else gains is <vocabulary form="やってあげる">to do (for someone)</vocabulary>, the outward giving inside <reading>やってあげる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 時間がないなら、その仕事は私がやってあげますよ。
example_sentences.english: If you don't have time, I'll do that job for you.
example_sentences.furigana: 時[じ]間[かん]がないなら、その仕[し]事[ごと]は私[わたし]がやってあげますよ。

example_sentences.japanese: 弟の宿題をやってあげたら、母に叱られました。
example_sentences.english: I did my little brother's homework for him and got scolded by Mom.
example_sentences.furigana: 弟[おとうと]の宿[しゅく]題[だい]をやってあげたら、母[はは]に叱[しか]られました。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女が忙しそうだったので、洗濯をやってあげました。
example_sentences.english: My girlfriend looked busy, so I did the laundry for her.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]が忙[いそが]しそうだったので、洗[せん]濯[たく]をやってあげました。

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Someone doing a favor for me: yatte kureru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Back on the <reading>yacht, a crew</reading> of borrowed hands bails the flooded hull while you only hold the tiller. Someone else doing the work for you, while you sit back, is <vocabulary form="やってくれる">to do (for me)</vocabulary>, the inward favour inside <reading>やってくれる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 病気で寝ていたとき、隣の人が買い物をやってくれた。
example_sentences.english: When I was sick in bed, my neighbor did the shopping for me.
example_sentences.furigana: 病[びょう]気[き]で寝[ね]ていたとき、隣[となり]の人[ひと]が買[か]い物[もの]をやってくれた。

example_sentences.japanese: 父はいつも、面倒くさいことを笑ってやってくれる。
example_sentences.english: Dad always does the tedious stuff for me with a smile.
example_sentences.furigana: 父[ちち]はいつも、面[めん]倒[どう]くさいことを笑[わら]ってやってくれる。

example_sentences.japanese: 会議の準備は、全部田中さんがやってくれました。
example_sentences.english: Tanaka-san did all the preparation for the meeting for us.
example_sentences.furigana: 会[かい]議[ぎ]の準[じゅん]備[び]は、全[ぜん]部[ぶ]田中[たなか]さんがやってくれました。

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Receiving the favor of an action: yatte morau.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Off the <reading>yacht, a moray</reading> eel is the only thing that will chew the fouled anchor rope free, so down it goes to do the job. Getting someone else to do the work in your place is <vocabulary form="やってもらう">to have (someone) do</vocabulary>, the sound sitting inside <reading>やってもらう</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 難しい問題は、専門家にやってもらいましょう。
example_sentences.english: Let's leave the difficult part to an expert.
example_sentences.furigana: 難[むずか]しい問[もん]題[だい]は、専[せん]門[もん]家[か]にやってもらいましょう。

example_sentences.japanese: 面倒くさい仕事は弟にやってもらった。
example_sentences.english: I got my little brother to do the tedious job.
example_sentences.furigana: 面[めん]倒[どう]くさい仕[し]事[ごと]は弟[おとうと]にやってもらった。

example_sentences.japanese: 自分でできないので、店員さんにやってもらいました。
example_sentences.english: I couldn't do it myself, so I had the shop clerk do it.
example_sentences.furigana: 自[じ]分[ぶん]でできないので、店[てん]員[いん]さんにやってもらいました。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 作（つく）＋ってあげる.
items.mnemonic_text: Making something and giving it: tsukutte ageru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="作">make</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="作ってあげる">to make (for someone)</vocabulary> word are the same word, so at heart it just means make. The tail on the end only adds that you make the thing for someone else, not for yourself.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 作 is 「つく」 from 作る, the verb it first appeared in, so <vocabulary form="作ってあげる">to make (for someone)</vocabulary> is <reading>つくってあげる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、彼女に弁当を作ってあげるつもりです。
example_sentences.english: Tomorrow I'm planning to make a boxed lunch for my girlfriend.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、彼[かの]女[じょ]に弁[べん]当[とう]を作[つく]ってあげるつもりです。

example_sentences.japanese: 夫が風邪なので、私が晩ご飯を作ってあげました。
example_sentences.english: My husband has a cold, so I made dinner for him.
example_sentences.furigana: 夫[おっと]が風邪[かぜ]なので、私[わたし]が晩[ばん]ご飯[はん]を作[つく]ってあげました。

example_sentences.japanese: 子供に紙で小さい箱を作ってあげましょう。
example_sentences.english: Let's make a little paper box for the kids.
example_sentences.furigana: 子[こ]供[ども]に紙[かみ]で小[ちい]さい箱[はこ]を作[つく]ってあげましょう。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 見（み）＋せてくれる.
items.mnemonic_text: Someone showing something to me: misete kureru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A friend makes you <kanji form="見">see</kanji> something by holding it up in front of your face. That small favour, done for you, is to <vocabulary form="見せてくれる">show (to me)</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 見 is 「み」 from 見る, the verb to look, so <vocabulary form="見せてくれる">to show (to me)</vocabulary> is <reading>みせてくれる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 祖父が古い写真を見せてくれました。
example_sentences.english: My grandfather showed me some old photos.
example_sentences.furigana: 祖[そ]父[ふ]が古[ふる]い写[しゃ]真[しん]を見[み]せてくれました。

example_sentences.japanese: 駅員さんが地図を見せてくれたので、道が分かりました。
example_sentences.english: The station attendant showed me a map, so I figured out the way.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]員[いん]さんが地[ち]図[ず]を見[み]せてくれたので、道[みち]が分[わ]かりました。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日のノート、ちょっと見せてくれる？
example_sentences.english: Could you show me your notes from yesterday for a sec?
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]のノート、ちょっと見[み]せてくれる？

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 教（おし）＋えてもらう.
items.mnemonic_text: Receiving the favor of being taught: oshiete morau.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="教">teach</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="教えてもらう">to have (someone) teach</vocabulary> word are the same word, so they carry the same meaning.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 教 is 「おし」 from 教える, the verb to teach, so <vocabulary form="教えてもらう">to have (someone) teach</vocabulary> is <reading>おしえてもらう</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 隣の人に駅までの道を教えてもらいました。
example_sentences.english: The person next to me told me the way to the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 隣[となり]の人[ひと]に駅[えき]までの道[みち]を教[おし]えてもらいました。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎週土曜日、姉に料理を教えてもらっています。
example_sentences.english: Every Saturday, my older sister teaches me how to cook.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]週[しゅう]土[ど]曜[よう]日[び]、姉[あね]に料[りょう]理[り]を教[おし]えてもらっています。

example_sentences.japanese: 分からない漢字は、先生に教えてもらったほうがいいですよ。
example_sentences.english: You'd better have your teacher explain the kanji you don't know.
example_sentences.furigana: 分[わ]からない漢[かん]字[じ]は、先[せん]生[せい]に教[おし]えてもらったほうがいいですよ。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 書（か）＋いてあげる.
items.mnemonic_text: Writing something and giving it: kaite ageru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="書">write</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="書いてあげる">to write (for someone)</vocabulary> word are one and the same, so the meaning does not change.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 書 is 「か」 from 書く, the verb to write, so <vocabulary form="書いてあげる">to write (for someone)</vocabulary> is <reading>かいてあげる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 祖母は目が悪いので、私が手紙を書いてあげます。
example_sentences.english: My grandmother's eyesight is poor, so I write her letters for her.
example_sentences.furigana: 祖[そ]母[ぼ]は目[め]が悪[わる]いので、私[わたし]が手[て]紙[がみ]を書[か]いてあげます。

example_sentences.japanese: 外国人のお客さんに、ホテルの住所を紙に書いてあげた。
example_sentences.english: I wrote the hotel's address on a piece of paper for a foreign guest.
example_sentences.furigana: 外[がい]国[こく]人[じん]のお客[きゃく]さんに、ホテルの住[じゅう]所[しょ]を紙[かみ]に書[か]いてあげた。

example_sentences.japanese: 息子の名前をカタカナで書いてあげたら、とても喜びました。
example_sentences.english: When I wrote my son's name in katakana for him, he was really happy.
example_sentences.furigana: 息子[むすこ]の名[な]前[まえ]をカタカナで書[か]いてあげたら、とても喜[よろこ]びました。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 手（て）＋伝（つだ）＋ってくれる.
items.mnemonic_text: Someone lending a hand for me: tetsudatte kureru.
items.furigana: 手伝[てつだ]ってくれる
